title: The Five Languages of Praise
author: Admired Leadership
summary: Riffing on Gary Chapman's Five Love Languages, this piece argues that praise, like affection, lands differently depending on how the recipient prefers to receive it. The author sketches five hypothetical 'praise languages' and uses them to challenge the Golden Rule as a guide for recognition. The central claim is that leaders who praise everyone the way they themselves like to be praised risk missing the mark, sometimes irritating the very people they intend to motivate. The fix is a shift from a blanket approach to an individualized one: learn how each team member prefers to be recognized and adapt accordingly. The piece closes with the line 'one size fits one' as its organizing metaphor for personalized recognition.
points: Praise, like love, is received differently by different people, so a single default style of recognition will land well for some and poorly for others.
The Golden Rule is a flawed guide for praise because it assumes everyone wants what you want.
Leaders should learn each team member's preferred 'praise language' rather than applying one uniform style across the team.
Tailoring recognition to the individual increases the odds it will motivate rather than merely land flat or even irritate.
quotes: Chapman emphasized that people tend to go wrong by showing love the way they prefer to receive it and not the way others want it.

This idea turns the Golden Rule on its head. “Do unto others as you would have them do unto you” is a good guide but can blind us to the reality that people often prefer to receive things in ways that we don’t.
Knowing how others prefer to receive praise, or not, is a great way of adapting your style to fit the person.
Adapting the way you give praise to team members recognizes their uniqueness.
That’s worth the effort it takes to avoid the blanket approach of praising everyone in the same way.
